implementation_notes: Go is the language where you should not write lock-free algorithms. The idiom is channels (a hchan is a ring buffer with two wait queues and a lock, and the runtime maintains it) and sync.Map / sync.Pool, both of which the runtime team wrote and tuned. Go's scheduler adds the one thing a hand-written lock-free algorithm cannot have: cooperative preemption at a function-call boundary, which means a spin loop in Go can starve the whole runtime, and runtime code must call Gosched. The GC also removes the memory-reclamation problem entirely, which is the hardest part of the discipline. sync/atomic's sequential consistency and the typed wrappers give the primitive if you need one, but reach for a channel first.
idiom_name: channels and sync.Map / sync.Pool (runtime-maintained), not hand-rolled lock-free structures
pitfalls: A hand-written spin loop without runtime.Gosched starves every other goroutine - Go's scheduler cannot preempt a goroutine that never reaches a blocking call.
Channel sends to a nil channel block forever, which is the idiomatic way to disable a select case but a deadlock when it is an accident.
An unbuffered channel is a rendezvous and changes the scheduling behaviour of both sides; a buffered one is a queue with real capacity semantics.
sync.Map is optimised for read-mostly or append-only key sets; for a write-heavy workload a plain map with a mutex is faster.
alternative: A channel for hand-off (the runtime's own ring buffer with wait queues), sync.Map for a concurrent map, and a mutex for genuinely shared mutable state
